extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology; clergy and seminary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critical survey of Catholic doctrinal positions on predestination, election, and reprobation, including definitions, theological corollaries, historical positions, and competing theories (ante/post praevisa merita, compromise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three senses of predestination
rubrics_metrics.description: Predestination may mean (1) predestination to receive certain graces (praedestinatio ad gratiam tantum); (2) predestination to enjoy eternal happiness without regard to any merits of his own (praedestinatio ad gloriam tantum); or (3) predestination to both grace and glory (complete or adequate predestination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing predestination, distinguish these meanings carefully; the dogma under consideration is primarily the complete (adequate) predestination (grace as means, glory as end). Theologians also speak of incomplete or inadequate predestination when grace and glory are considered separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (adequate) predestination — components
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete predestination involves: (a) the first grace of vocation (gratia prima praeveniens), especially faith as the beginning of justification; (b) a number of additional actual graces for the process; (c) justification itself as the beginning of the state of grace; (d) the grace of final perseverance; (e) eternal happiness in Heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list enumerates the successive stages that constitute adequate predestination; doctrines about election should account for vocation, sustaining graces, justification, perseverance, and final beatitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholic dogma: eternal predestination of the elect
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catholic Church has always taught the eternal predestination of the elect as an article of faith: God’s eternal foreknowledge and decree dispose the elect to salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dogma affirms an eternal decree linked with God’s foreknowledge and the successive stages of calling, justification and glorification (cf. Rom. 8:28–30). Opposing views (Pelagian, Semi-Pelagian) are rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immutability of the divine decree of predestination
rubrics_metrics.description: The divine decree of predestination is immutable: God’s unerring foreknowledge and will fix who is to be rewarded with eternal happiness; the ‘Book of Life’ admits neither addition nor erasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the decree is immutable in God’s knowledge, Scripture and theology allow that human cooperation (prayer, works) can change a person’s hypothetical status into an actual destiny—i.e., one may, by cooperation with grace, change God’s hypothetical decree concerning oneself into an absolute realization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of the elect is definitively fixed (absolute/relative distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the divine decree is immutable, the number of the elect must be definitively fixed; God knows both the abstract number and each individual predestined to Heaven, though humans cannot know the precise number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes absolute number (known only to God) and relative estimations (some argue few are saved; others hold majority will be saved). Theological speculation on exact numbers is uncertain and disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive and causes of predestination
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficient cause of predestination is God; the instrumental cause is grace; the final cause is the divine glory; the primary meritorious cause is the merits of Jesus Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These causal categories are agreed upon among theologians and should be invoked when explaining the origins and purpose of predestination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of human merits on predestination — initial vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Human merits exert no influence on predestination to the initial grace of vocation; initial vocation is absolutely gratuitous and cannot be based on prior natural merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserting any natural merit as the motive for initial vocation contradicts the doctrine of the gratuity of grace (per St. Thomas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of natural merits on predestination to grace and glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural merits do not influence predestination to grace and glory: since grace is absolutely gratuitous, the union of grace and glory cannot be based upon natural merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments defending the gratuity of predestination seek to avoid making grace a reward of natural merits (a Pelagian error). Historical debates often aimed to safeguard this gratuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate over supernatural merits and predestination (ante vs post praevisa merita)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a theological controversy whether predestination to glory is (a) absolutely decreed by God without regard to future supernatural merits (predestination ante praevisa merita) or (b) decreed in view of God’s foreknowledge of those merits (predestination post praevisa merita).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both positions are set forth with arguments; the lack of decisive Scriptural/Patristic texts means Catholic opinion is divided. Exposition should present both theories impartially and examine their arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of absolute predestination (ante praevisa merita)
rubrics_metrics.description: This theory holds that, in the order of intention, God by an absolute decree predestines certain men to salvation and then decides to give them the graces necessary to be saved; in the order of execution He bestows graces then rewards glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated by many Thomists and some Augustinians; supported by certain scriptural readings and Augustine. Critics argue it risks implying positive reprobation (Calvinistic conclusion), is weak on Patristic support, and may commit petitio principii in philosophical defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of hypothetical predestination (post praevisa merita)
rubrics_metrics.description: This view holds predestination is conditional: God elects to eternal life those whose good use of the gifts He foresaw (predestination depends on foreseen merits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favored by Greek Fathers and many theologians outside the Thomist school; argued to harmonize with Scripture’s universality of God’s saving will and with the biblical portrayal of rewards granted on account of works (e.g., Matth. XXV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise (eclectic) theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A middle position holds that while the common run of humanity is predestined hypothetically, a few exceptionally favored saints (e.g., the Blessed Virgin, prophets, apostles, all infants dying in baptism) enjoy absolute predestination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theory has some historical proponents but is criticized for making the salvation of most elect a matter of chance and lacking strong Revelation or reason support; special exception is often made only for the Blessed Virgin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprobation defined and limits (no positive reprobation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprobation is God’s foreknowledge of the wickedness of some creatures and the preparation of their damnation; there can be no absolute and positive predestination to eternal punishment (positive reprobation would be heretical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theologians distinguish reprobation as foreknowledge/preparation rather than an active divine causation of sin; Catholic councils (e.g., Second Council of Orange, Trent) condemn positive predestinarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive reprobation (heretical predestinarianism) — characteristics and condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive reprobation asserts an unconditional divine decree causing certain persons to be damned (Calvinist/predestinarian position). This is condemned as heretical by Catholic councils and theologians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists historical proponents (Calvin, Wiclif, etc.) and argues this view contradicts Scripture’s universality of saving will, the bestowal of sufficient grace to all, and the divine attribute of holiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative reprobation (Thomist formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative reprobation is an eternal decree by which God excludes from Heaven those not absolutely predestined — i.e., determines not to save them — without asserting He positively wills their damnation or causes their sins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomist theologians articulate negative reprobation as a pure negation (exclusion) rather than as positive imposition of punishment; defenders locate the ultimate reason for exclusion in original sin or divine sovereign will without implying God causes sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for Scriptural and Patristic argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural passages must be interpreted in context (e.g., Romans IX is obscure and not an unambiguous locus classicus for absolute predestination); Patristic evidence is mixed (Greek Fathers favor hypothetical predestination; Augustine is contested and claimed by both sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal claims about predestination should not press ambiguous texts beyond their context, and must weigh Patristic testimony critically; neither Scripture nor Tradition yields conclusive proof for all disputed theories, so balanced exposition is required.
